lesson.title: Concentration Units: Many Rulers for the Same Measurement
lesson.summary: Concentration units such as mass percent, parts per million, and mole fraction are different precise ways to state how much solute is present in a given amount of solution.
lesson.body:
Once solvent and solute are defined and a solution's saturation state is understood, chemistry needs a precise, numeric way to say exactly how much solute is packed into how much solution, not just "unsaturated" or "concentrated." Several different units exist for this because different situations call for different levels of precision or convenience.

Mass percent is the simplest: mass of solute divided by mass of solution, times 100. It shows up constantly on real labels, since normal saline used in medicine is about 0.9% NaCl by mass, and household bleach is typically around 6% sodium hypochlorite by mass.

For very dilute solutions, mass percent produces awkward tiny decimals, so parts per million takes over: ppm equals mass of solute divided by mass of solution, times 1,000,000. It is the standard unit for trace contaminants, like reporting lead or chlorine levels in drinking water.

Mole fraction, written using the Greek letter chi, is moles of one component divided by total moles of every component in the mixture, and it becomes essential later for relating vapor pressure to solution composition, since it directly compares particle counts rather than masses.

A single worked example ties mass percent and ppm together. Dissolve 2.50 g of a solute in enough solvent to make 250.0 g of total solution. Mass percent equals 2.50 g divided by 250.0 g, times 100, which is 1.00%. The same solution in ppm is 2.50 g divided by 250.0 g, times 1,000,000, which is 10,000 ppm. Those two answers describe the identical solution and are self consistent, since 1% always equals 10,000 ppm by definition.

The most important concentration unit in a chemistry laboratory, moles of solute per liter of solution, gets its own full treatment next, because computing it correctly requires bringing in the mole concept in a way the units above do not.
